primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Acute coronary plaque disruption with superimposed thrombosis abruptly reduces myocardial blood flow, producing ischemic myocyte necrosis and release of cardiac troponin.
vignette: A 61-year-old man has 50 minutes of crushing substernal chest pressure radiating to his left arm with diaphoresis and nausea. ECG shows new ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Serum cardiac troponin is elevated.
distractor_notes: Stable angina causes predictable exertional ischemic pain without myocardial necrosis or persistent ST elevation and troponin rise.
Acute pericarditis typically causes pleuritic positional chest pain with diffuse ST elevation and PR depression rather than a territorial inferior pattern.
Aortic dissection usually causes abrupt tearing pain radiating to the back and does not by itself produce this classic territorial ST-elevation pattern.
Gastroesophageal reflux can cause chest discomfort but does not explain ST-segment elevation and elevated cardiac troponin.
key_expl: Prolonged ischemic chest pain with territorial ST elevation and elevated troponin establishes an acute STEMI.
objective: Diagnose acute STEMI from prolonged ischemic symptoms, territorial ST elevation, and myocardial-injury biomarkers.
clues: inferior ST elevation and elevated troponin

sources.title: Heart Attack
sources.support: NHLBI describes heart attack as myocardial injury from blocked coronary blood flow and notes characteristic symptoms, ECG changes, and cardiac biomarkers.

sources.title: Heart attack
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes acute myocardial infarction as blockage of blood flow to heart muscle causing chest pain and myocardial damage.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Endothelial dysfunction permits LDL entry and modification in the arterial intima; macrophages ingest modified lipoproteins through scavenger receptors and become foam cells, initiating fatty streaks.
vignette: A 48-year-old man with smoking, hypertension, and elevated LDL cholesterol has an asymptomatic carotid plaque. Histology of an early lesion shows lipid-laden macrophages in the arterial intima.
lead: These foam cells most directly arise from which process?
correct: Macrophage uptake of modified LDL particles
distractors: Smooth-muscle uptake of chylomicrons through pancreatic lipase
Platelet synthesis of cholesterol from bile acids
Endothelial conversion of HDL into LDL
distractor_notes: Neutrophils are not the principal foam-cell population in early atherosclerotic fatty streaks.
Chylomicron processing occurs mainly through lipoprotein lipase; pancreatic lipase acts in the gut and does not create arterial foam cells.
Platelets do not synthesize plaque cholesterol from bile acids.
HDL is not converted into LDL by endothelial cells; modified LDL accumulation and macrophage uptake drive foam-cell formation.
key_expl: Macrophages take up oxidized or otherwise modified LDL through scavenger receptors, becoming lipid-laden foam cells in early atherosclerotic lesions.
objective: Explain foam-cell formation in atherosclerosis as macrophage uptake of modified LDL in the arterial intima.

sources.title: Atherosclerosis
sources.support: NHLBI describes cholesterol-rich plaque formation in arterial walls and the role of inflammatory cells in atherosclerosis.

sources.title: Atherosclerosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes atherosclerosis as buildup of fats, cholesterol, and other substances in artery walls.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Autosomal dominant pathogenic variants in sarcomeric proteins such as beta-myosin heavy chain cause myocyte hypertrophy and disarray, often producing asymmetric septal hypertrophy and dynamic outflow obstruction.
vignette: A 19-year-old athlete has exertional syncope. Echocardiography shows marked asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. His father died suddenly at age 36.
lead: A pathogenic variant in which protein is a common cause of this disorder?
distractor_notes: Dystrophin defects cause Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy and can cause dilated cardiomyopathy rather than classic HCM.
Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome and aortic disease.
CFTR defects cause cystic fibrosis.
Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome and basement-membrane disease.
key_expl: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is commonly caused by autosomal dominant variants in sarcomeric genes including MYH7, which encodes beta-myosin heavy chain.
objective: Associate familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with pathogenic variants in cardiac sarcomere proteins.
clues: asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion
family history of sudden cardiac death

sources.title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as commonly caused by variants in sarcomere genes and associated with ventricular hypertrophy and sudden death risk.

sources.title: MYH7 gene
sources.support: MYH7 encodes beta-myosin heavy chain, a major cardiac sarcomere protein; pathogenic variants can cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss-of-function KCNH2 variants reduce the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current, delaying ventricular repolarization and predisposing to torsades de pointes.
vignette: A 16-year-old girl has recurrent syncope triggered by sudden loud noises. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. Genetic testing identifies a pathogenic KCNH2 variant.
lead: The affected protein normally conducts which ion?
distractors: Sodium exclusively through the fast inward current
Hydrogen ions through an ATP synthase
distractor_notes: KCNH2 encodes a potassium channel rather than a chloride channel.
Fast sodium current is mediated by channels such as SCN5A, not KCNH2.
L-type calcium channels are distinct proteins and are not encoded by KCNH2.
KCNH2 is a plasma-membrane cardiac ion channel, not mitochondrial ATP synthase.
key_expl: KCNH2 encodes the hERG potassium channel that contributes to ventricular repolarization; reduced current prolongs the QT interval.
objective: Connect KCNH2 loss of function with reduced cardiac potassium current and delayed ventricular repolarization.

sources.title: Long QT syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes long QT syndrome as delayed cardiac electrical recovery due to ion-channel abnormalities, including KCNH2 variants.

sources.title: KCNH2 gene
sources.support: KCNH2 encodes a cardiac potassium channel important for repolarization.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
mechanism: Reduced cardiac output activates sympathetic signaling and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, increasing vasoconstriction and sodium-water retention but chronically worsening remodeling and congestion.
vignette: A 70-year-old man with prior myocardial infarction has an ejection fraction of 28%, pulmonary edema, and elevated plasma renin activity.
lead: Which physiologic response most directly explains the increase in plasma renin?
correct: Reduced renal perfusion pressure at the juxtaglomerular apparatus
distractors: Increased sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa
Increased atrial natriuretic peptide signaling at juxtaglomerular cells
Expansion of effective arterial blood volume
Suppression of renal sympathetic nerve activity
distractor_notes: Increased macula densa sodium chloride delivery suppresses rather than stimulates renin release.
Natriuretic peptide signaling opposes renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation.
Heart failure reduces effective arterial perfusion despite total-body fluid excess, so effective arterial volume is not expanded at the kidney.
Renal sympathetic activation stimulates renin; suppression would reduce it.
key_expl: Low cardiac output reduces effective renal perfusion, stimulating juxtaglomerular renin release and downstream RAAS activation.
objective: Explain RAAS activation in systolic heart failure as a response to reduced effective renal perfusion.

sources.title: Heart Failure
sources.support: NHLBI describes heart failure as inadequate cardiac pumping with compensatory neurohormonal responses and fluid retention.

sources.title: Heart failure
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes reduced pumping function, congestion, and neurohormonal responses in heart failure.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: After birth, systemic vascular resistance exceeds pulmonary resistance, so a nonrestrictive ventricular septal defect initially produces a left-to-right shunt and increased pulmonary blood flow.
vignette: A 2-month-old infant has a large ventricular septal defect and signs of congestive heart failure. Oxygen saturation is initially normal in the systemic arterial circulation.
lead: What is the predominant direction of blood flow across the defect early in life?
distractors: Pulmonary artery to aorta through the ductus arteriosus
No net flow because ventricular pressures are identical
distractor_notes: Right-to-left flow typically occurs only after severe pulmonary vascular disease reverses the shunt or when right-sided pressure exceeds left-sided pressure.
An atrial shunt occurs across an atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale, not a ventricular septal defect.
Ductus arteriosus flow is anatomically separate from a VSD.
A large VSD can partially equalize pressures, but systemic-to-pulmonary pressure and resistance differences still generate net left-to-right flow early.
key_expl: Postnatal systemic pressure is greater than right-ventricular/pulmonary pressure, producing an initial left-to-right VSD shunt.
objective: Predict the early postnatal direction of flow through a ventricular septal defect from relative ventricular pressures.

sources.title: Ventricular Septal Defect
sources.locator: What it is; effects on blood flow
sources.support: CDC describes a VSD as an opening between the ventricles that allows extra blood to pass to the lungs.

sources.title: Ventricular septal defect
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes VSD as an opening between the ventricles that commonly increases pulmonary blood flow.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Inflammation of the pericardium produces pleuritic positional chest pain and diffuse epicardial electrical injury, classically causing widespread ST elevation and PR-segment depression.
vignette: A 27-year-old man develops sharp chest pain 1 week after a viral respiratory illness. The pain worsens with inspiration and lying supine and improves when he sits forward. ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression.
distractor_notes: Inferior myocardial infarction causes territorial ST elevation in contiguous inferior leads and ischemic pressure-like pain rather than diffuse ST elevation with positional pleuritic pain.
Stable angina is exertional, transient, and does not cause persistent diffuse ST elevation or PR depression.
Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic pain but usually does not cause diffuse ST elevation with PR depression and positional relief.
Aortic dissection causes abrupt severe tearing pain and lacks the classic pericarditic ECG pattern.
key_expl: Positional pleuritic pain relieved by sitting forward plus diffuse ST elevation and PR depression is classic acute pericarditis.
objective: Diagnose acute pericarditis from its characteristic chest-pain quality and diffuse ECG pattern.
clues: diffuse ST elevation with PR depression

sources.title: Pericarditis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes pericarditis as inflammation causing sharp chest pain that may improve when sitting up and leaning forward.

sources.title: Pericarditis
sources.support: NHLBI describes pleuritic positional chest pain and ECG abnormalities in acute pericarditis.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Congenital narrowing of the aortic arch or proximal descending aorta raises proximal arterial pressure while reducing lower-extremity perfusion and can produce collateral intercostal flow.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for hypertension. Blood pressure is 158/88 mm Hg in both arms and 108/66 mm Hg in the legs. Femoral pulses are delayed compared with radial pulses.
distractor_notes: Patent ductus arteriosus causes continuous flow between the aorta and pulmonary artery and typically produces bounding pulses rather than upper-lower extremity pressure disparity.
Atrial septal defect produces a left-to-right atrial shunt without radiofemoral delay.
Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanosis from right-to-left shunting rather than isolated upper-extremity hypertension with weak femoral pulses.
Pulmonary valve stenosis affects right-ventricular outflow and does not cause a marked arm-leg blood pressure gradient.
key_expl: Upper-extremity hypertension with lower-extremity hypotension and radiofemoral delay is classic for aortic coarctation.
objective: Recognize coarctation of the aorta from differential upper- and lower-extremity blood pressure and delayed femoral pulses.
clues: arm hypertension with lower leg pressure

sources.title: Coarctation of the Aorta
sources.locator: Signs and effects on blood flow
sources.support: CDC describes coarctation as narrowing of the aorta that can cause high blood pressure before the narrowing and reduced blood flow beyond it.

sources.title: Coarctation of the aorta
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes upper-extremity hypertension, weak femoral pulses, and reduced lower-body perfusion in coarctation.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of functional hepatic LDL receptors reduces receptor-mediated endocytosis and plasma clearance of LDL particles, producing markedly elevated LDL cholesterol and premature atherosclerosis.
vignette: A 28-year-old man has tendon xanthomas and an LDL cholesterol concentration of 315 mg/dL. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 41. Genetic testing shows a pathogenic LDLR variant.
lead: Which cellular process is most directly decreased?
correct: Receptor-mediated uptake of circulating LDL by hepatocytes
distractors: Hydrolysis of triglycerides in chylomicrons by lipoprotein lipase
Cholesterol esterification within HDL by LCAT
Mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids
distractor_notes: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes severe hypertriglyceridemia and chylomicronemia, not isolated marked LDL elevation.
LCAT participates in HDL cholesterol esterification and is not the primary defect in LDLR-related familial hypercholesterolemia.
Copper excretion is mediated by ATP7B and is defective in Wilson disease.
Medium-chain fatty-acid oxidation is impaired in MCAD deficiency and does not explain extreme LDL elevation.
key_expl: LDLR encodes the hepatic LDL receptor; reduced receptor function decreases LDL uptake and clearance from plasma.
objective: Explain severe LDL elevation in familial hypercholesterolemia through impaired hepatic LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis.
clues: tendon xanthomas with very high LDL
premature coronary disease in first-degree relative

sources.title: Familial hypercholesterolemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes familial hypercholesterolemia as a disorder of impaired LDL clearance causing very high LDL and early cardiovascular disease.

sources.title: LDLR gene
sources.support: LDLR encodes the LDL receptor, which binds and internalizes LDL particles for clearance, especially in the liver.
